title: OIDC Resource Owner Password Credentials (ROPC)
subtitle: ⛔ DEPRECATED — the app collects the user's raw password and posts it to the token endpoint; forbidden by OAuth 2.1 and the Security BCP. Documented here only so you can recognize it and migrate to Authorization Code + PKCE.

steps.label: User types password into the app
steps.lede: The user enters their username and password directly into the client application — not into the IdP's own login page. Handing the raw password to the app is the defining flaw of this grant.
steps.devtools: There is no /authorize step and no redirect in ROPC — the whole flow is a single back-channel POST. That absence of an IdP-hosted login page is itself the warning sign.

steps.label: POST /token grant_type=password
steps.lede: The client posts the credentials to the token endpoint. The username and password travel in the request body in cleartext; a confidential client also sends its own credentials via Authorization: Basic.
steps.devtools: ⛔ This is the deprecation red flag. Open the request's Payload tab: grant_type=password with username and password in cleartext. Anything that can read the request — a proxy, a browser extension, an over-broad log — sees the password. This is exactly why OAuth 2.1 forbids ROPC. Always redact a real capture; migrate the client to Authorization Code + PKCE.

steps.label: Validate credentials against the directory
steps.lede: The AS checks the username and password against its user directory. On success it mints tokens; on failure it returns a deliberately field-agnostic error.
steps.devtools: The AS validation happens server-side. Note what it cannot do here: there is no interactive channel, so it can't run an MFA challenge or a password-change prompt — those failure modes all collapse into a single 400 (see below).

steps.label: 200 — tokens returned
steps.lede: The AS returns an access token, a refresh token, and — because openid was requested — an ID token. Note there is no nonce anywhere: ROPC has no /authorize step to carry one.

jwt.title: Decoded id_token
payload: The legacy client the token was minted for

steps.devtools: Decode the id_token payload. There is no nonce — ROPC has no /authorize step to bind one, which is one of its weaknesses. The refresh_token should be disabled or rotated aggressively: it extends the reach of a grant that already mishandled the password.

steps.label: Wrong password → 400 invalid_grant
steps.lede: A bad password is rejected with a field-agnostic error that never reveals whether the username or the password was wrong.
steps.devtools: A 400 invalid_grant with a generic "invalid username or password" is deliberate — it does not say which field was wrong, to avoid username enumeration.

steps.label: MFA required → 400 interaction_required
steps.lede: Even with a valid password, policy may require a second factor. This grant has no interactive channel to carry an MFA challenge, so it simply fails — forcing a switch to a redirect-based flow.
steps.devtools: A 400 with interaction_required means the AS wants a second factor (or a password change) that this grant cannot carry. The only fix is to move the client to Authorization Code + PKCE, where the IdP's own pages can run the challenge. This is the concrete reason ROPC is a dead end.
